```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Mixture models explain heterogeneity in a population by assuming that it
consists of a small number of unobserved subpopulations, the latent classes,
each with its own pattern of responses. In latent profile analysis the
pattern is a set of means of continuous indicators, and in latent class
analysis it is a set of response probabilities of categorical indicators.
When observations are nested in groups, the groups themselves can differ.
Course enrolments, for example, are nested within students, and one student
may be engaged in most of their courses while another is engaged in few. A
two-level model captures such differences with a second set of latent
classes, the group classes. Each group class is a type of student, defined by
the proportions of the student's enrolments that fall in each profile. For a
given number of classes, the model estimates how large each class is and what
its response pattern looks like. The number of classes itself is an input to
the estimation, and the model returns no estimate of it. The analyst fixes
the number of profiles, and in a two-level model the number of group classes,
before estimation, and every substantive conclusion of the analysis depends
on that choice.

Choosing the number of classes is difficult because the usual tools for
comparing models each fall short in a specific way. Fit alone always favours
more classes, since a model with one more class can reproduce the smaller
model and improve on it. The likelihood ratio test, which compares nested
models in most settings, gives invalid p-values here. A model with k classes
is a model with k + 1 classes in which one class has size zero, and at that
edge of the parameter space the test statistic loses its usual reference
distribution. Valid p-values then require simulating many data sets from
the smaller model and refitting both models to each, which is slow when many
candidates are compared. Information criteria avoid testing altogether and
instead balance fit against a charge for every estimated parameter. The
criteria differ in that charge, so the Akaike information criterion, with a
light charge, tends to favour more classes than the Bayesian information
criterion, with a heavier one.

Applied data raise further problems. In large samples even the
Bayesian information criterion often keeps decreasing as classes are added,
because small departures from the model become detectable and each new class
absorbs some of them. The lowest value then falls on the largest model that
was fitted, and the size of each improvement says more than the position of
the minimum. In a two-level model the number of profiles and the number of
group classes are chosen together, and the charge of the Bayesian information
criterion depends on whether the sample size counts the students or their
enrolments. Finally, a model can fit the data well and still separate its
classes poorly, so that many enrolments or students sit between classes, and
its estimate can be a local maximum of the likelihood that a different
starting point would improve.

This document applies class enumeration to a two-level latent profile model.
Every combination of the requested numbers of profiles and group classes is
fitted with `enumerate_classes()`, and every fitted model is kept. Each
candidate is described by its information criteria under both definitions of
the sample size, by the decrease of a criterion with each added profile and
each added group class, by the knee of each of these curves, by the
certainty of its classification and by checks of its estimation. Selected
candidates are then compared side by side. The chosen candidate is taken
from the fitted candidates for further analysis.

The evidence is reported in full because no single statistic determines the
number of classes. The criteria, the changes between candidates and the
classification quality together show where additional classes stop improving
the model. A choice made from this evidence can be stated, justified and
reproduced from the reported tables.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

```{r data-values, include = FALSE}
n_enrolments <- nrow(course_engagement)
n_students <- with(course_engagement, length(unique(student)))
```

## Data

The examples use `course_engagement`, a data frame in long format with one
row per course enrolment. It contains
`r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments of `r n_students`
students. Five measures of activity in each course serve as indicators:
browsing of the course site, lecture viewing, reading of the forum, posting
to the forum and attendance. Each measure is standardized within its course,
so a value of zero is the course average. The column `student` identifies the
student to whom each enrolment belongs.

```{r data}
head(course_engagement)
```

Enrolments are nested in students. The profiles therefore describe patterns
of activity in a single course, and the group classes describe students by
how their enrolments are distributed across those patterns.

## Fitting the candidate models

The candidates are fitted with `enumerate_classes()` from the data, the
indicators in `vars` and the group identifier in `id`. The arguments
`n_profiles` and `n_group_classes` give the numbers of classes to try, and
one model is fitted for every combination of them. Here the numbers of profiles run from one to six and the numbers of
group classes from one to four. The argument `model` sets the covariance
structure of the profiles. The value `"VVI"` gives every profile its own
variances and fixes the covariances at zero. Without `model`, the four basic
structures are fitted for every combination.

The likelihood of a mixture model has several local maxima, so each model is
estimated from several random starts and the solution with the highest
likelihood is kept. The argument `n_starts` sets the number of starts. The
example uses three starts per model to keep the computation short. Applied
analyses use ten or more. The argument `seed` makes the starts reproducible.
With many starts, a candidate with too many profiles can reach a solution in
which one profile sits on a single observation with every variance at its
lower bound; its likelihood is then set by `min_variance`, not by the data.
`boundary = "exclude"` sets such starts aside (see *Checks of the
estimation*). A profile with fewer members than its own means and variances
is reported by a `latents_thin_profiles` warning, as in the grid below,
because its solution may be spurious. `search = "emEM"` screens five times as
many starts by short EM runs and continues the best; it reaches the highest
maximum more often, and also spurious maxima more often. Large grids take time; `cores` fits the candidates in parallel
and returns the same result as one core.

```{r enumerate}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models
```

```{r models-values, include = FALSE}
candidates <- as.data.frame(models)
n_candidates <- nrow(candidates)
n_failed <- with(candidates, sum(is.na(log_likelihood)))
best <- get_results(models, "best")
pick <- function(name, convention_name) {
  with(subset(best, criterion == name & convention %in% convention_name),
       candidate)
}
bic_groups_pick <- pick("bic", "groups")
bic_individual_pick <- pick("bic", "individuals")
icl_groups_pick <- pick("icl", "groups")
awe_groups_pick <- pick("awe", "groups")
aic_pick <- with(subset(best, criterion == "aic"), candidate)
# The code below names these candidates; stop if the results ever change.
stopifnot(bic_groups_pick == "profiles4_groups3",
          icl_groups_pick == "profiles4_groups2",
          awe_groups_pick == "profiles3_groups2")
```

The result holds `r n_candidates` fitted candidates. Each candidate is named
by its numbers of profiles and group classes, so that `profiles4_groups3` has
four profiles and three group classes, and the name identifies the candidate
in every function that follows. The `r n_failed` candidates with one profile
and several group classes could not be estimated. Group classes are defined
by differences in the distribution of profiles, and a model with a single
profile has no such differences. These candidates remain in the table with
the error that stopped them.

## The table of candidates

The table of candidates has one row per candidate and is returned by
`as.data.frame()`.

```{r table}
as.data.frame(models)
```

The columns fall into groups.

| Columns | Content |
|---|---|
| `candidate`, `n_profiles`, `n_group_classes`, `model` | Identity of the candidate |
| `log_likelihood`, `n_parameters` | Fit and size |
| `aic`, `kic`, `bic_*`, `sabic_*`, `caic_*`, `awe_*`, `icl_*`, `clc_*` | Information criteria |
| `profile_entropy`, `group_entropy` | Relative entropy at each level |
| `avepp_min`, `avepp_max`, `avepp_mean`, `avepp_below` | Average posterior probability of the profiles |
| `group_avepp_min`, `group_avepp_max`, `group_avepp_mean`, `group_avepp_below` | Average posterior probability of the group classes |
| `converged`, `boundary`, `n_best_replicated`, `warnings`, `error` | Checks of the estimation |

## Information criteria

An information criterion is the deviance, minus twice the maximized
log-likelihood, plus a charge for every estimated parameter. Lower values
indicate a better balance of fit and complexity. In a two-level model the
charge of several criteria depends on the sample size. Criteria ending in
`_groups` count the `r n_students` students as the independent units, and
criteria ending in `_individual` count the
`r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments. An analysis uses one of
the two conventions throughout.

The candidate at the minimum of each criterion:

```{r best}
get_results(models, "best")
```

The criteria disagree. With students as the units, the Bayesian information
criterion (BIC) is lowest for `r bic_groups_pick`, the integrated completed
likelihood (ICL) for `r icl_groups_pick` and the approximate weight of
evidence (AWE) for `r awe_groups_pick`. With enrolments as the units, BIC is
lowest for `r bic_individual_pick`. The Akaike information criterion (AIC) is
lowest for `r aic_pick`, the largest candidate fitted, because its light
charge per parameter keeps it decreasing across the whole range.

The criteria are plotted against the number of profiles, one line per number
of group classes, with the lowest value of each criterion ringed.

```{r plot-criteria, fig.height = 5}
plot_enumeration(models)
```

A minimum at the largest number of profiles or group classes fitted shows
that the criterion is still decreasing there. The range of the candidates is
then widened until the minimum lies inside it. Any criterion can be plotted
by name, and `what = "all"` plots every criterion.

```{r plot-bic}
plot_enumeration(models, what = "bic_groups")
```

The tree plots how the profiles divide as more are added. Each profile of a
model is linked to the profiles of the next model that receive its
observations. Each number of group classes has its own tree, and
`n_group_classes` selects one; `plot_tree(models)` returns them all, one plot
each. The guide *Tree plot* compares solutions at one number of profiles and
plots the tree of group classes.

```{r plot-tree, fig.height = 6}
plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)
```

## Change with each added class

When a criterion decreases across the whole range, the size of each decrease
becomes the evidence. For every candidate, the table reports the decrease in
BIC from the candidate with one profile fewer and the same number of group
classes, and the decrease from the candidate with one group class fewer and
the same number of profiles. A positive value means that the added class
lowered the criterion. The argument `using` selects another criterion.

```{r deltas}
get_results(models, "deltas")
```

```{r deltas-values, include = FALSE}
deltas <- get_results(models, "deltas")
delta_of <- function(name) {
  with(subset(deltas, candidate == name), round(delta_profile))
}
step_3 <- delta_of("profiles3_groups3")
step_4 <- delta_of("profiles4_groups3")
step_5 <- delta_of("profiles5_groups3")
stopifnot(step_3 > 0, step_4 > 0, step_5 < 0)
```

With three group classes, adding a third profile lowers BIC by
`r format(step_3, big.mark = ",")` and adding a fourth lowers it by
`r format(step_4, big.mark = ",")`. Adding a fifth profile raises BIC by
`r format(-step_5, big.mark = ",")`, which appears in the table as a negative
decrease. The decreases are plotted for both directions, along the
number of profiles on the left and along the number of group classes on the
right.

```{r plot-deltas, fig.height = 5}
plot_selection(models, what = "deltas")
```

The knee summary scales both axes of a curve to the unit interval and finds
the candidate with the largest perpendicular distance below the straight
line from the first point to the last. This chord-distance rule is inspired
by Kneedle, without its smoothing or sensitivity thresholds. A nearly linear
curve can have a very small maximum distance, so the reported distance
describes the strength of the bend as well as its location. The knee is computed
along the number of profiles for each number of group classes, along the
number of group classes for each number of profiles, and across all
candidates ordered by their number of parameters.

```{r knees}
get_results(models, "knees")
```

```{r knee-values, include = FALSE}
knees <- get_results(models, "knees")
profile_line <- subset(knees, direction == "profiles" &
                         line == "3 group classes")
knee_along_profiles <- with(profile_line, knee_candidate)
knee_without_largest <- with(profile_line, knee_without_largest)
knee_along_groups <- with(subset(knees, direction == "group_classes" &
                                   line == "4 profiles"), knee_candidate)
```

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is
`r knee_along_profiles`. The straight line ends at the largest
candidate, so the knee depends on the range fitted. Without the largest
candidate the knee is `r knee_without_largest`, which the
table records in `stable` and `note`. Along the number of group classes with
four profiles, the knee is `r knee_along_groups`.

The criterion over all candidates at once, as the distance of each from the
lowest value:

```{r heatmap}
plot_selection(models, what = "heatmap")
```

## Classification quality

Every observation has a posterior probability of membership in each class.
Relative entropy summarizes these probabilities over all observations, from 0
when every observation is equally likely to belong to every class, to 1 when
every observation belongs to one class with certainty. The average posterior
probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean posterior probability of that
class among the observations assigned to it. An AvePP of 0.7 or 0.8 and
above is commonly taken to indicate adequate separation. The table of
candidates reports the lowest, highest and mean AvePP at each level and the
number of classes below a cutoff, which is 0.8 by default and is set with
`cutoff`.

```{r quality}
plot_selection(models, what = "diagnostics")
```

The AvePP of every class of every candidate, with its size and the relative
entropy of its level:

```{r classification}
get_results(models, "classification")
```

```{r quality-values, include = FALSE}
chosen_row <- subset(candidates, candidate == bic_groups_pick)
profile_entropy_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(profile_entropy, 2))
group_entropy_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(group_entropy, 2))
avepp_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(avepp_min, 2))
group_avepp_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(group_avepp_min, 2))
```

For `r bic_groups_pick`, the relative entropy is
`r profile_entropy_chosen` for the profiles and `r group_entropy_chosen` for
the group classes. The lowest AvePP is `r avepp_chosen` among the profiles
and `r group_avepp_chosen` among the group classes.

## Checks of the estimation

A solution reached from several random starts is more credible than a
solution reached once, because a single start may have stopped at a local
maximum. An estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, such as a
variance at its lower bound, indicates a model too complex for the data. A
class that holds a very small share of the observations is also hard to
interpret. A candidate on the boundary whose smallest profile holds about one
observation is not a profile but a degenerate solution; refitting with
`boundary = "exclude"` keeps, for every candidate, the best start without a
variance at its lower bound. The following plots report these checks for
every candidate.

```{r trust}
plot_selection(models, what = "trust")
```

```{r smallest}
plot_selection(models, what = "smallest")
```

All of the plots for choosing the number of classes are produced together
with `plot_selection(models)`.

## Comparing candidates

Selected candidates are placed side by side with `compare_models()`.
Candidates are named as in the table, given by their numbers of classes, or
selected by a number of profiles or group classes. The comparison adds the difference in
BIC from the lowest of the candidates compared and the BIC weight. The weight
is `exp(-delta_bic / 2)` normalized to sum to one, the approximate posterior
probability of each candidate when all have equal prior probability.

The candidates preferred by BIC, ICL and AWE with students as the units:

```{r compare-names}
compare_models(models, bic_groups_pick, icl_groups_pick, awe_groups_pick)
```

The same candidates given by their numbers of classes, with labels:

```{r compare-counts}
compare_models(models, bic = c(4, 3), icl = c(4, 2), awe = c(3, 2))
```

Every candidate with four profiles, which shows what the group classes add:

```{r compare-select}
comparison <- compare_models(models, n_profiles = 4)
comparison
plot(comparison)
```

The comparison keeps the fitted models. The AvePP of every class of every
compared model is returned by `get_results()`, and the model behind a row by
`get_candidate()`.

```{r compare-classification}
get_results(comparison, "classification")
```

## Analysis of the chosen candidate

The example continues with `r bic_groups_pick`, the candidate with the lowest
BIC with students as the units. It is taken from the fitted candidates by
name with `get_candidate()`. The numbers of classes give the same model, as
in `get_candidate(models, 4, 3)`.

```{r chosen}
chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen
```

`chosen` is the same kind of object that `multilpa()` returns. Its summary
reports the estimates with their standard errors.

```{r chosen-summary}
summary(chosen)
```

The profiles are plotted as their means on the five indicators.

```{r chosen-profiles}
plot_profiles(chosen)
```

Each group class of students has its own distribution of the four profiles.

```{r chosen-prevalence}
plot_prevalence(chosen)
```

The classification diagnostics of the chosen model:

```{r chosen-diagnostics}
diagnostics(chosen)
```

```{r chosen-diagnostic-plots, fig.height = 7}
plot_diagnostics(chosen)
```

Each enrolment with its profile, its student's group class and its posterior
probabilities:

```{r chosen-assignments}
head(get_results(chosen, "assignments", data = course_engagement))
```

The profiles can be related to an outcome. The mean of `previous_grade` in
each profile is estimated with `three_step()`, which corrects for the
uncertainty of the classification with the BCH method.

```{r chosen-outcome}
three_step(chosen, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
```

## Functions

```{r reference, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Call = c(
    "enumerate_classes(data, vars, id, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model)",
    "as.data.frame(models)",
    "get_results(models, \"best\")",
    "get_results(models, \"classification\")",
    "get_results(models, \"candidates\", cutoff = 0.9)",
    "get_results(models, \"deltas\", using = )",
    "get_results(models, \"knees\", using = )",
    "plot_enumeration(models), plot_enumeration(models, what = \"bic_groups\"), what = \"all\"",
    "plot_tree(models)",
    "plot_enumeration(models, what = \"entropy\", \"avepp\" or \"diagnostics\", cutoff = )",
    "plot_selection(models, what = \"deltas\", \"heatmap\", \"smallest\" or \"trust\", using = )",
    "plot_selection(models)",
    "get_candidate(models, \"profiles4_groups3\"), get_candidate(models, 4, 3)",
    "compare_models(models, \"name\", c(4, 2), ...)",
    "compare_models(models, n_profiles = , n_group_classes = )",
    "compare_models(name = fit, name = fit)",
    "get_candidate(comparison, \"name\")",
    "get_results(comparison, \"classification\")"),
  Result = c(
    "The fitted candidate models",
    "One row per candidate with every column",
    "The candidate at the minimum of each criterion",
    "Size, AvePP and entropy of every class of every candidate",
    "The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff",
    "Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer",
    "Maximum chord-distance knee of each line, its range and its stability",
    "Information criteria across the candidates",
    "Division of profiles as more are added",
    "Entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates",
    "Decreases, distance from the lowest criterion, smallest class, estimation checks",
    "All of the plots for choosing the number of classes",
    "One fitted candidate",
    "Named candidates side by side",
    "All candidates with the given numbers of classes",
    "Fitted models side by side, on the same data",
    "The model behind a row of a comparison",
    "Every class of every compared model")),
  col.names = c("Call", "Result"))
```
